schools.summary: Ellicott studies the double name: the chronicler calls him Uzziah (Azariah only at 1 Chron 3:12), but the Assyrian inscriptions of Tiglath-pileser call him Azriyahu; he was known by both names, to foreigners chiefly as Azariah.
Clarke sketches the whole reign in advance: a pious and prosperous beginning, then the invasion of the priest's office, leprosy, and abdication to Jotham.
Matthew Henry frames the moral: Uzziah kept the pure worship of God and (unlike his father) shunned idols, and as long as he sought the Lord God made him to prosper.
Gill notes only that this is the king called Azariah elsewhere and refers to the parallel.

Ellicott reads 'continued to seek God' as the chronicler's idiom and argues the true text is 'understanding in the fear of God' (with the versions, Rashi, Kimchi), not 'visions'; Zechariah was the king's guide in religion and politics alike.
Gill rules out the later prophet and the murdered Zechariah, taking this counsellor to be a son of the priest Joash slew.
Clarke knows Zechariah only by this character, a man skilled in the divine visions and probably the young king's tutor.
Henry warns that Uzziah sought God only while Zechariah lived, having no principle in himself to hold him to the end.

debates.question: Does the text read 'understanding in the visions of God' or 'in the fear of God'?

sides.position: 'visions of God' — skilled in interpreting the divine oracles
'fear of God' — the reading of the versions, Rashi and Kimchi, and doubtless correct

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott detail the campaign: Gath (taken by David), Jabneh (Jamnia/Jebnah, the Jabneel of Josh 15:11) and Ashdod (Esdud, guarding the road to Egypt) broken down and Judahite cities planted, reducing Philistia to vassalage though still under its own kings.
Gill marks the reversal — these were the Philistines who under Jehoram had broken in upon Judah (2 Chron 21:16).
Keil and Ellicott extend the divine help over Philistines, the Arabians of Gur-baal (an unknown site — Targum Gerar, LXX Petra) and the Mehunim/Maonites of Maon near Seir, made tributary.
Gill stresses that Uzziah conquered not by his own strength but by God's help, citing the Targum's 'the Word of the Lord helped him.'
Clarke likewise cites the Targum and identifies the Arabians as the Meunim/Meonites.

Ellicott and Keil read the Ammonite 'gifts' as tribute (minchah) and the name spreading 'to the entering in of Egypt' as the report of real victorious power reaching the frontier; 'strengthened himself' = showed strength, made head (cf. Dan 11:7).
Gill takes the Ammonites as tributaries or peace-seekers.
Clarke calls the gifts an annual tribute.

themes: fame to the border of Egypt
the seed of the coming pride

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott map the three fortifications — the corner gate (NW), the valley gate (the modern Jaffa gate, W), and the tower at the 'turning of the wall' (the SE angle of Zion joining the temple hill, per Neh 3:19) — the quarters most open to attack.
Gill notes the corner gate, broken down under Amaziah, repaired and crowned with a tower.
Henry adds that Uzziah's best fortification was his adherence to God's worship — had his father not forsaken it, the wall would never have been broken.

themes: the vulnerable sides of the city
true defence is fidelity to God

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott set the towers and cisterns in the wilderness of Judah and the trans-Jordan Mishor (Reuben's land, recovered from Moab and Ammon), where his herds grazed; 'he loved husbandry' = a lover of the soil.
Clarke calls love of husbandry a perfection in a king on which every state depends; Wesley reads the towers as guarding the cattle from Arabian raids and warning of enemies.
Gill sets the desert towers as walled refuges (like pagodas) for shepherds and flocks against robbers.
Henry paints a king who delighted not in war or sport but in the quiet employments of the husbandman, honouring the calling.

themes: towers and cisterns in the desert

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott expound the muster: the host went out in bands/troops (each house a troop) by a census (pequddah) drawn up by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer under Hananiah, one of the king's captains.
Gill notes plainly that Uzziah had a standing army.
Henry sees two establishments — a field host for reprisal raids and a garrison army for defence.

Keil and Ellicott read the 2,600 as the heads of fathers'-houses, valiant heroes, over the larger army beneath them, the host marshalled by clans with the bravest chief leading each house's detachment.
Gill takes them for the commanders and principal officers, implying a very large army under them.
Keil and Ellicott describe the 307,500-strong force that 'made war with mighty power,' agreeing roughly with Amaziah's 300,000 (2 Chron 25:5), each chief over about 120 men.
Gill notes the army exceeded his father's by 7,500 besides officers.
Henry stresses the overwhelming might — no enemy durst face them — grounded in Uzziah's great armoury.

themes: mighty power to help the king

schools.summary: Ellicott sorts the armoury — shields, spears, helmets and habergeons for the heavy-armed; bows and slings for the light — and reads 'stones of slings' as proof the equipment was complete.
Henry notes the arms were both offensive and defensive, and that swords go unmentioned because every man wore his own.
Gill stresses the arms were prepared for every soldier throughout the host.
Clarke reads a strategist's foresight — weapons kept in readiness for any emergency.

Keil calls the engines ingenious slinging machines like Roman catapults and ballistas for shooting arrows and stones; Ellicott names them the first mention of artillery, figured on Assyrian sculptures and passed thence to Palestine.
Clarke claims this the first record of siege-engines anywhere, the Jews their inventors ~800 B.C., before which sieges dragged for years (Samaria, Nineveh, Troy).
Gill argues from Pliny and Diodorus that such engines were invented in Judea, not Greece or Rome.
Henry laments that men's lusts made cunning men devise instruments of death.

themes: marvellously helped till he was strong
skill turned to instruments of death

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott read Uzziah as seeking to unite king and high priest in one person, like the Egyptian Pharaohs; Ellicott renders 'to his destruction' as 'dealing corruptly,' doubts the David/Solomon precedent, and sets it beside Saul (1 Sam 13:9) and the law of Num 18:1-7.
Henry makes this the one blot on Uzziah, rooted in pride of heart — the prosperity of fools destroys them; his sin was intruding into the temple, not forsaking it.
Clarke says he assumed the priest's office; Wesley specifies he entered the holy place where none but priests might come, much less offer incense.

debates.question: Was Uzziah reviving a royal precedent of David and Solomon in offering incense?

sides.position: no — those kings organised the ritual but never performed the distinctive priestly functions; this was fresh usurpation
the act was plain pride and unlawful intrusion, condemned by the law

themes: the great High Priest of our profession

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott present the high priest Azariah (probably the man of 1 Chron 6:10) and eighty priests, 'sons of valour' — so called for the moral courage to withstand the king — insisting that incense belongs only to Aaron's consecrated line.
Gill identifies Azariah as the high priest, going in to hinder and persuade the king.

Ellicott parses the charge — incense belongs to Aaron's consecrated sons, 'trespassed' echoing v.16, and 'not for thine honour' meaning the act will end in shame; Keil carries the narrative on to the leprosy and expulsion.
Wesley stresses they withstood him only by admonition, not force (the censer stays in his hand), and modestly, honouring him still as sovereign.
Gill notes they stood about him, surrounding him to block his approach to the altar.

Ellicott renders the king's 'foaming' rage, the censer in hand (Ezek 8:11), and the leprosy that 'rose up' beside the altar — the stroke of Miriam (Num 12:10) and Gehazi (2 Kings 5:27) — with the Josephus embellishments of earthquake and sunbeam.
Wesley reads the leprosy as a blow from an invisible hand from the altar, that Uzziah might know it the direct effect of God's displeasure.
Henry: had he submitted all had been well, but his wrath drew God's wrath — those who will not see by the judgment of God's mouth are made to see by the judgment of his hand.
Gill notes his anger and (from Josephus) his threat to kill the priests.

debates.question: Was the leprosy truly a divine judgment on Uzziah's offence, or only a traditional interpretation the chronicler adopted?

sides.position: a real stroke from God's own hand upon the sin
the chronicler followed traditional exegesis in making the leprosy a judgment, though the invasion itself was historical

themes: the stroke of Miriam and Gehazi

schools.summary: Ellicott sharpens the Hebrew — the priests 'turned towards him,' 'thrust him out' (scared/hurried, cf. Esther 6:14), and he 'thrust himself' out — because the Lord had smitten him (2 Kings 15:5).
Henry sees a flicker of the fear of God: the king who strove with the priests would not strive with his Maker, and fled the moment he knew God was angry.
Wesley notes no force was needed — the king hasted away under the priests' persuasions and warnings of further judgment.
Gill notes the leprosy, though over all his body, showed most remarkably in his forehead where all could see it.

Ellicott renders the 'several house' a lazar-house and expounds the chronicler's added clause 'cut off from the house of the Lord' — excluded as a leper by the law of Lev 13:46, he had to isolate from all society.

Clarke notes the separation from all society and Jotham's regency; Wesley reads the incurable leprosy as a lasting monument of God's anger and draws the exact correspondence — thrust from the temple he had usurped, deprived of the throne that was rightly his.
Henry: a leper is dead while he lives, buried alive; those who covet forbidden honours forfeit the honours that were lawfully theirs.
Gill notes he was a leper till death, dwelling in a separate house.

themes: cut off from the house of the Lord

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott attribute the fuller record to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, Ellicott noting Kings instead cites 'the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.'
Clarke observes Isaiah's history of Uzziah is wholly lost — the king is barely named in the surviving book (Isa 1:1; 6:1).
Gill notes the record covered his acts first and last.

themes: Kings versus Chronicles on the source
what the Spirit chose to keep

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott explain he was buried not in the royal tombs but in the burial-field near them, lest a leper's body defile the sepulchres; Kings says only 'in the city of David.'
Clarke gives the same reason — a leper barred from the common royal burying-place lest even the grave be defiled.
Gill dates his death (with Lightfoot) to the year of his smiting, and recalls that Isaiah's temple vision (Isa 6:1) fell in the year of the king's death.

themes: the stigma carried to the grave

schools.summary: Keil reads the rebuilding of Elath as completing Amaziah's subjection of Edom and the base for later campaigns; Ellicott stresses the emphatic 'it was he who built' and identifies Eloth as the Idumean Red Sea port, noting these verses stand identical with Kings.
Clarke notes the port's history and that the king bears several names.

themes: mastery of Edom and the sea
